title: Mom looks for her daughter
example: At a family dinner Maria asks 'where is Lia?'. Lia lives in the same household, so she is one link away from Maria and the very first person Maria checks.
why: Target is a direct neighbor of the start node (depth 1). BFS finds it in the first pass, so the work is O(1) no matter how big the rest of the family tree is.

title: Grandpa calls his son at the reunion
example: Grandpa Ramon wants to call his son Carlos at a reunion of 13 relatives across three generations. His own children are checked first, and Carlos is the first one he checks.
why: Same best case in a bigger tree: BFS explores closest relatives first, so a target one link away is found after about 2 operations out of 53.

title: Dad asks for his eldest child
example: In a busy household with grandparents, an uncle's family and four kids, Arman just asks 'where is Cris?'. His children are the first people he checks.
why: Target is a direct neighbor of the start (depth 1) in a family of 14 people. BFS looks at close relatives first, so it stops after about 3 operations out of 58.

title: Finding a first cousin
example: Eli wants a ride to the reunion from his cousin Hugo. They share grandparents Lito and Mina, so BFS must go up to the grandparents and back down the other branch.
why: Target is 4 links away (up two generations, down two). BFS explores roughly half of the family before reaching it: average case, still O(V+E) but only part of it.

title: Two families meet at a wedding
example: At the wedding of Carl and Gina, the groom wants to find the bride's brother Hector. The two families are only connected through the marriage, so the search crosses the spouse link first.
why: Target sits in the other family, 3 links away across a marriage. About half of the combined family is explored before it is found.

title: Four generations: finding a second cousin
example: Lou joins a family-history website and wants to contact Quin, a second cousin. Their branches only meet at great-grandparents Abe and Bea, three generations up.
why: 20 people over four generations. The target is 6 links away (up three, down three), so BFS checks close relatives and most cousins first: about 73% of the work.

title: Finding grandma's sister for a family photo
example: Xavi wants to invite his great-aunt Rosa, the sister of his grandmother Quim. He must go up to his parents, his grandparents and his great-grandparents Odon and Pia before coming down to Rosa.
why: Target is 4 links away (up three generations, down one). BFS explores about half of the family before it reaches her.

title: Meeting a new stepbrother
example: Sal's mother Rina married Uli, who already has a son, Vic, from an earlier marriage. Sal wants to message his new stepbrother, and the path goes through both parents.
why: Target is 3 links away across a remarriage (Sal - Rina - Uli - Vic). About a third to a half of the blended family is explored first.

title: Tracing ancestry back 8 generations
example: Hugo traces his lineage back to the founding ancestor Ansel, who emigrated eight generations ago. Every generation has a couple and one child, so the tree is a long chain.
why: Target is the deepest node (7 links away). BFS must expand almost every relative on the way, so it does nearly all of the work (about 87%).

title: Searching for someone who is not related
example: A church registry holds two unrelated families. Searching Rey's family for Zed (who belongs to the other family) means checking every relative before BFS can say 'not found'.
why: Target is not connected to the start, so BFS explores the whole connected family and only then reports not found: the full O(V+E) cost, 100%.

title: The newest baby of a large clan
example: A clan reunion with four branches and 26 people. Zed is the newest baby, seven links away from Hal on the farthest branch, so every other branch is checked first.
why: Target is the deepest node in a wide and deep tree. BFS expands every closer relative before reaching it, about 90% of the work in either neighbor order.

title: A name missing from the family registry
example: A clerk searches Aldo's family for Zara, but Zara was never linked to anyone (a person with no relatives in the file). Every relative is checked before BFS reports not found.
why: Target has no links at all, so it can never be reached. BFS must explore the entire connected family: the full cost, 100%. (A lone person is written as a line with only person_a.)
